extracted.intended_audience: health-care journalists, editors, and PR professionals who write or evaluate news about medical tests, treatments, products, and procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and checklist for evaluating or producing news stories and press releases about health-care interventions, focused on patient-centered questions about benefits, harms, evidence quality, costs, conflicts, novelty, availability, and independence of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story adequately discuss the costs of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the story addresses the financial cost of the treatment/test/product/procedure so readers can judge affordability and trade-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes this criterion received the most unsatisfactory scores in long-term reviews. News stories that omit costs do not sufficiently help patients and consumers. Include out-of-pocket costs, insurance implications, and comparative costs when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story adequately quantify the benefits of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the story provides numeric estimates of how effective the intervention is, using appropriate measures (absolute and/or relative) and clear framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers want to know 'How effective is it?' Report absolute benefits where possible and explain the meaning of effect sizes and clinical relevance. Beware of framing that overstates benefit by using only relative risk reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story adequately explain/quantify the harms of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the story reports the possible harms, side effects, risks, and their frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coverage emphasizes benefits while minimizing harms, it is misleading. Provide numeric harm rates, severity, and context so readers can weigh benefits vs harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story seem to grasp the quality of the evidence?
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the story communicates how rigorous and reliable the supporting evidence is for the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain study design (randomized trial vs observational), sample size, endpoints, replication, and limitations. Readers should get a sense of how robust the evidence is and whether claims are tentative or well-established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story commit disease-mongering?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the story exaggerates or invents conditions, medicalizes normal states, or expands disease definitions to create demand for interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for turning risk factors into diseases (e.g., low bone density → osteoporosis), medicalizing aging or normal variations (baldness, wrinkles, shyness), or overstating prevalence/severity to justify interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story use independent sources and identify conflicts of interest?
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that the story includes objective, independent third-party experts and discloses any financial or other conflicts of interest of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers deserve to know if researchers or spokespeople stand to benefit financially, are paid consultants, or otherwise have COIs. Balance promotional sources with independent experts to contextualize claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story compare the new approach with existing alternatives?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the story situates the new intervention relative to current standard treatments, tests, or nonmedical options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just because something is new doesn't mean it's better. Reporters should mention other options, comparative effectiveness, and whether the new approach offers meaningful advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story note the availability of the treatment/test/product/procedure?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the story informs readers whether and how the intervention is actually available to patients now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New interventions often receive attention before they are widely available. State whether the product is approved, in trials, commercially available, limited to research centers, or not yet accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story establish the true novelty of the approach?
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the story accurately reports what is genuinely new about the intervention and whether novelty implies improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether the intervention is truly innovative or a minor variation, and whether any novelty translates into improved outcomes. Distinguish novelty from marketing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story appear to rely solely or largely on a news release?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check if reporting is based mainly on a PR news release with little or no original reporting, verification, or independent sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that rely heavily on press releases often fail other criteria (no costs, no harms, no independent sources). Reporters should disclose reliance on releases and add independent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing study results using relative rather than absolute risk reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when coverage frames benefits using relative risk reductions that exaggerate impact without providing absolute risk figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing is a common flaw that makes interventions seem more effective than they are. Always prefer or include absolute risk reductions and numbers-needed-to-treat where relevant, and explain baseline risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting surrogate endpoints without explaining limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect when stories present results measured on surrogate endpoints or markers without clarifying their limitations and uncertain link to meaningful clinical outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrogate endpoints (e.g., lab measures) may not translate into real health benefits. Reporters should explain what the surrogate measures and whether outcomes on surrogates have proven patient-centered benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using causal language for observational study results
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag coverage that inappropriately implies causation from observational research that can only show associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studies are observational, reporters must explain limitations, potential confounding, and avoid stating that the exposure 'caused' the outcome unless randomized trials support causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting based on single source or undisclosed conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate if a story relies primarily on one source—particularly one with undisclosed COIs—or if the reporter or outlet has accepted value from that source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-source stories are vulnerable to bias, especially when the source has a financial stake. Disclose COIs and seek independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: The tyranny of the anecdote (single-anecdote stories used as PR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify stories that hinge on a single compelling patient anecdote that may function as a public relations tool rather than representative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes can mislead when they are presented without data or context. Balance human stories with population-level evidence and state how typical the anecdote is.

rubrics_metrics.name: News releases on nutrition, supplements, and 'natural' interventions tend to be promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation from release reviews that PR for nutrition and supplement products is often less evidence-based and more promotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These releases frequently provide little or questionable data; reporters should be especially skeptical, request primary data, and seek independent experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: News releases about new cancer tests frequently oversell claims and omit COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding that many PR releases for new cancer tests misled readers with exaggerated claims, omitted conflicts of interest, and lacked justification for assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should scrutinize test performance metrics, seek independent validation, and demand disclosure of financial ties and limitations before amplifying test claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General pattern: PR-driven stories often lack data, disclosure, and independent reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary assessment that stories and releases reliant on PR commonly fail multiple criteria (no costs, no harms, no independent sources, overselling benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HealthNewsReview project graded items as 'satisfactory', 'unsatisfactory', or 'not applicable' and found many PR-driven pieces scored poorly. Use the full criteria checklist to push editors for fuller coverage and transparency.
